 Garmin's website currently shows that the company makes 26 different watches. That's a lot. And on the surface, they're all pretty similar. They come in multiple sizes and color variations, but working out which is the best Garmin watch is a slog.
 That's why I've narrowed your choice down to just five options. I've been testing Garmin watches for years, including during training for, and running, marathons, so I know what separates a good one (strong battery life, accurate tracking) from the rest.
 Whether you're getting into Garmin for the first time or need a watch that'll support your running, my top pick right now is the Garmin Forerunner 570 . It's not the cheapest, but for around the cost of an Apple Watch you get an incredible amount of features bundled into an impressively durable wearable.
 If you're looking to keep the cost down, the Forerunner 170 is my favorite budget-friendly Garmin watch. It's not actually the cheapest in the range, but it only costs a fraction more and is easily the best value Garmin watch, making it perfect for beginners.
 But these aren't your only choices. I've collected the best Garmin watches for a range of uses and budgets together. Plus, if these six don't quite hit what you're after, check out all the other models we've tested for some more options, too.

 The Garmin name is pretty much synonymous with running, which is why the Garmin Forerunner 570 is the best Garmin watch we've tested and the best Garmin watch for runners.
 I should qualify what I mean by best here: this is the best watch that I think you should buy right now, but in technical terms, the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro is the best. Though, it's also double the price and has so many features you probably won't use that the 570 is a better value option for most people.
 It has a dazzling AMOLED display and comes in a wider range of colors than we usually see from Garmin, including watches with eye-catching yellow and pink bezels. It comes in two sizes — 42mm and 47mm — and offers runners everything they need to track and analyze their training.
 While you miss out on some features available on pricier Garmin watches like the Forerunner 970 , like maps and running economy measurements, the Forerunner 570 has everything you need to run marathons and beyond, all in an attractive and lightweight package.
 The watch has a 1.4-inch AMOLED display, which is as large a screen as you’ll find on any Garmin sports watch aside from the Venu X1 , and it’s bright enough to be clear in all conditions even on the lowest brightness setting. This bright display does have a downside; it reduces the battery life of the watch.
 But at 10 days, it's still a far sight better than even the best Apple Watches , which generally can only make it a single day between charges. Plus, the GPS is reliably accurate, and the Elevate V5 heart rate sensor is impressively precise.
 You also get detailed training insights including VO2 max estimates, race time predictions, training load analysis and advice on how well acclimated to heat and altitude you are. The Forerunner 570 also has Garmin’s Training Readiness feature, which rates how ready to train you are each day.

 The Garmin Forerunner 170 is the follow up to the Forerunner 165 , which for the past few years has been the best budget Garmin you can buy. The Forerunner 170 doesn't stray from that path, but includes a lot more training and sports analysis than the 165 did, turning it from a good watch to a great one, especially for beginners.
 It inherits sports features that have normally been the reserve of Garmin's premium watches, including a load of team, racket and winter sports options. It's a similar story with training analysis, with premium features like Training Status, Readiness and Training Load analysis hitting the budget-friendly watch for the first time.
 The Forerunner 170 has a new Quick Workout option for runners too, which will suggest training sessions based on how hard you want push yourself and how long you have. Our reviewer is a regular marathon runner, but found that some of the sessions were too intense, so he scaled them back to make them more attainable.
 The smartwatch-style strengths of the 165 are retained, with access to contactless payments through Garmin Pay and offline streaming service playback (Spotify or Deezer) if you choose the slightly more expensive Forerunner 170 Music edition. And, like every Garmin, you can access the Connect IQ app store.
 As it's a cheaper watch in Garmin's range, it has the slightly older Elevate Gen 4 heart rate sensor, which is the same as the Forerunner 165. It'll serve you well, but we've found the Gen 5 is generally more accurate (compared to a heart rate strap) and the use of Gen 4 means you don't get ECG or skin temperature sensors on the 170.
 One area to be cautious of (and this applies to all the best Garmins) is the battery life. The company says you'll get 11 days between charges in the lightest use case, during testing with reasonable everyday usage and run tracking, we found it closer to three or four days. Still, it's a lot better than the single day of the best Apple Watches .

 The Garmin Lily 2 Active doesn't offer nearly as many trackable sports profiles as most of the other devices in our guide nor do you get Garmin's higher-end training tools, like Garmin Coach. But, it's perfectly suitable for keeping tabs on popular exercises like runs, walks, gym workouts, yoga, pilates and, of course, pickleball.
 The specs say you should get nine days from the battery, or nine hours with GPS tracking on, which we found to be right on the money. And the display is the biggest battery drain: at max brightness, we lost 30% in one day, but slowed the drain by switching to the auto-brightness setting.
 Additionally, the Lily 2 Active offers 24/7 heart rate monitoring, SpO2 tracking and Garmin’s Body Battery feature to help you gauge your energy levels throughout the day. It additionally keeps tabs on stress, sleep quality and menstrual cycles.

 Aside from all the extra features and improved battery life, the reason we recommend the Lily 2 Active is that it's only $50 more than the standard model, but offers so much for that extra cost that it makes the Lily 2 and Lily 2 Classic seem a bit pointless.

 Charging devices is a chore, and also impractical if you're on the go or out on the trail. So if extending your Garmin watch's battery life is the most important factor you, the Garmin Instinct 3 is the best model to go for.
 The base model lasts up to 18 days between charges, and can reach 32 hours in GPS-only mode. But the most interesting version of the watch is the Solar edition, which integrates a solar charging panel to extend the battery further.
 Assuming you have enough light to charge it, the watch can keep itself topped up without a dedicated charger and reach up to 260 hours in GPS-only mode on the larger 50mm model (compared to the 45mm's 130 hours).
 To make all this work, there are some compromises (other than the fairly large design). There's no touchscreen, so you only interact with the watch using the five physical buttons. This sounds fine, but there is a learning curve.
 The buttons have different functions depending on how long you press them, which we found wasn't super intuitive, but you do get used to it after a while. It doesn't have the latest heart rate sensor (the Elevate V5, as in the Fenix 8 ), but uses the V4, found in the older Fenix 7 and Instinct 2.
 Still, Instinct 3 offers many of Garmin's best training tools, including Body Battery, Training Readiness Score, in-depth sleep quality analysis, workout recovery time suggestions and blood oxygen saturation monitoring. However, there are no ECG readings.

 The Garmin Cirqa offers sleep, training, and recovery insights beyond those offered by competitors like the Fitbit Air, while being relatively budget-friendly at $199 upfront with no subscription price needed. Plus, it offers up to 10 days of battery life with a single charge.
 During testing, we found it fairly comfortable to wear, although it isn't the most slimline screenless fitness tracker in the world. Still, it's very lightweight, so it's not imposing to wear.
 The real standout feature of the Cirqa is its physical button that can be customized to track a workout type of your choosing. The Cirqa has support for 80 different workout types, so no matter what your regular workout type is, you'll be able to start tracking it with just a push of a button.
 While it does offer actionable workout insights, these insights aren't the most in-depth, so if you're very serious about fitness or a pro athlete, you may want to go for the Garmin Forerunner 570 .
 Another thing to keep in mind is that the Cirqa does not have onboard GPS, so you'll need to pair a phone needed to enable location tracking. Plus, while it does have auto workout tracking, it isn't the most reliable and does need a bit of user dedication to get it set up at first.

 How we test Garmin watches 
 We test the best Garmin watch models by strapping them to our wrists and wearing them during the day and overnight for several weeks. During this time, we're assessing every aspect of the device, including design and comfort, battery life claims, tracking accuracy and any new features or training tools.
 When it comes to comfort, some watches are pretty bulky, which means they may fit awkwardly on smaller wrists or prove burdensome for all-day wear. Design-wise, we're also paying attention to how the watch holds up to the daily bumps and bruises of daily life, including encounters with water.
 For athletes, a bright and easy-to-read screen is a must for checking stats while on the go, something we take into great account. Ease of use additionally gets consideration; are there physical buttons, a touchscreen, or a combo of both? We prefer the latter.
 When it comes to assessing fitness tracking features, we're all about putting the best Garmin watch models to the test against other proven devices. Sometimes that involves walking thousands of steps with a popular tracker on either wrist.
 During these head-to-head showdowns, we're not only comparing fitness stats from each watch but GPS tracking accuracy and battery efficiency as well. Post-workout, we dive into Garmin's training and recovery tools. Are the insights useful and actionable, or are they just stating the obvious?
 The same approach is taken when assessing sleep-tracking data. Do the results correlate with our perceived sleep quality? Finally, we try out any of the device's extra features, like mobile payments, onboard music storage, downloadable maps, and voice support.
 Once testing wraps up, all of this information, which includes a mix of qualitative impressions and quantitative comparisons gets condensed down into our review, at which point, the device is considered for inclusion in this buying guide.
 How to choose the best Garmin watch for you 
 One of the most crucial aspects of choosing a Garmin watch is thinking about what you'll use it for. If you run long marathons, battery life will be key. The same applies if you do outdoor adventures where you need GPS navigation, as that's a power-hungry feature.
 Once you've focused in on what you plan to do with your Garmin watch, it'll make it easier to choose between models. If you need specific running plans or metrics, narrow in on a model that can do that; often something from the Forerunner range.
 On the other hand, if you want to up your golf game, pick a watch from the Approach models. And if you need something that'll suit your training and everyday life, be on the lookout for which smartwatch features are supported.
 And it's important to note that not every watch in Garmin's range has a touchscreen or a bright display to rival the best smartwatches . Though there are several models that do allow you to download music to watch so you can connect your Bluetooth headphones and listen while you train, even if you don't have your phone.
 FAQs 
 What is Garmin Connect+?
 Garmin Connect+ is a subscription service that cost $70 annually, and gives you access to a performance dashboard and live activities for strength workouts. The main reason the company seems to have launched the service (other than recurring revenue) is to add 'AI-backed' insights, which currently have little utility. We tried Garmin Connect+ for a month , and despite loving Garmin watches, can't really say it's worth the money.
 Do all Garmin watches have GPS?
 No, not all Garmin Watch models have onboard GPS, but most do. All of the models in our buying guide boast GPS, which means that you won't need to carry a paired phone with you for location-tracking data. 
 Garmin models that don't have GPS include the standard Lily 2 and the Vivosmart 5, which is more of a fitness tracker than a smartwatch. 
 Which Garmin watch models have maps?
 Only Garmin's higher-end watch models offer the ability to download and manage maps to your device for offline use. These include the Garmin Forerunner 965 (and 955), Enduro 3 (and Enduro 2), Fenix 8 (and Fenix 7) and the Garmin Epix series. 
 Which Garmin watch models can answer a phone call or text?
 A small selection of Garmin watches have built-in microphones and speakers, allowing you to take calls from the wrist via a Bluetooth-paired smartphone or dictate a message. These include the Garmin Venu 2 and 3, as well as the Garmin Fenix 8. 
 Some Garmin models offer the ability to send a quick reply from the wrist by selecting from a list of pre-written messages. However, this feature only works with Android devices. 
 Which Garmin watch is best for navigation?
 There are two types of navigation available in Garmin's range. Top-end models like the Fenix 8 and Forerunner 965 have offline maps and can create routes for you on the fly, or reroute you if you go off course. 
 Cheaper models like the Forerunner 170 and Garmin Instinct 3 offer breadcrumb navigation, with turn-by-turn instructions and a line and pointer to keep you on track, but no actual maps.
 Garmin's maps are the best navigation tool available on any sports watch and it's worth investing in a watch with them if that's a priority for you. If you're on a budget, then older watches with maps like the Garmin Epix 2 and Garmin Forerunner 955 are often in sales. 
 If possible, we recommend getting an AMOLED Garmin if you're going to use the maps a lot, as they are clearer on the AMOLED display, though this does reduce battery life compared to an MIP Garmin.
 Is Garmin better than Apple?
 Garmin and Apple watches have a lot of similar features, but excel in different areas. Garmin watches are better for battery life, sports tracking, training analysis and navigation, while Apple watches excel on design, fitness tracking and smart features in particular. Both are great options for sports tracking, but which is better will depend on your priorities. And, of course, the Apple Watch only works with iPhones, while you can use a Garmin on Android or iPhone. 
 How do I download Garmin Connect? 
 You'll need to download the Garmin Connect App to sync your watch to your phone. It's available on both Android and iOS . Once you've downloaded the app and signed up, you can begin the pairing process. 
 The Garmin Connect app lets you see all your data at a glance in an easy-to-read format. Depending on your tracker, it'll give you deeper insights, such as your body battery (based on your sleep data) and your fitness age. There are also challenges and in-depth sleep reports for you to keep an eye on.
 Additionally, depending on your Garmin model, you'll be able to use the Garmin Connect app to use Garmin Coach to download running and cycling training plans and upload them directly to your watch. Garmin Coach lives under the 'training' tab in the app and features loads of options to suit all abilities and goals.

 The Google Fitbit Edge is Google's latest fitness tracker, and it's designed as a halfway house between the screenless, super-cheap Google Fitbit Air and the full-fat Google Pixel Watch 5 smartwatch. Costing $179.99 / £159.99 / AU$269, it's packing GPS (which the Air doesn't) and Fitbit's improved automatic activity detection, alongside the usual metrics like heart rate, sleep tracking, and estimated calories burned.
 But is it accurate? That's the big question. While we found the Google Fitbit Air accurate compared to the Apple Watch Ultra 3 and a heart rate monitor, we've been burned by Fitbit in the past, with some accuracy issues plaguing this device's spiritual predecessor, the Fitbit Charge 6 .
 I've only been testing the Edge for a couple of days, but I wanted to test its mettle straight away. On my first 5km run with the new Fitbit, I compared its stats on one wrist against another wearable, the high-end Garmin Fenix 9 Pro .
 Latest Videos From TechRadar 
 Watch full video here: 
 The 9 Pro costs around five times as much as the Google Fitbit Edge, and has been tested against chest-mounted heart rate monitors and other premium wearables like the Apple Watch Ultra 4 to determine accuracy.
 It's worth noting that devices normally take a few days to learn your movement patterns and baseline metrics, so I was expecting some deviation in metrics such as heart rate. However, I was hoping the Google Fitbit Edge's distance and pace information, calculated via GPS, would cleave closely to the Fenix 9 Pro's metrics, as that would indicate the little fitness tracker is almost as accurate as the powerful Fenix 9, making it good value for money.

 Fitbit Edge leak reveals a new fitness tracker with a screen 
 I tested the Google Pixel Watch 5's GPS against Apple and Garmin 
 The results
 (Image credit: Future) When I compare wearables during workouts, I use the average heart rate metric as a good indication of wearable accuracy. Heart rate, measured by LED-based PPG sensor arrays, is the cornerstone of wearable health tracking and a core basis of everything from estimations in sleep quality to calorie burn.
 Average heart rate, which all wearables provide during a workout, is a great way to compare. While different devices use different algorithms and so forth, resulting in fluctuations in graphs, if two or more wearables show a similar average heart rate, it's a good indication that these devices are broadly accurate.

 Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
 Fortunately, the cheaper Google Fitbit Edge does cleave very closely to the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro, which I know is accurate thanks to past tests against the Frontier X2 heart rate monitor and Apple Watch Ultra 4. The Google Fitbit Edge showed an average heart rate of 156 bpm , while the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro showed an average heart rate of 153 bpm . That's a great result for the Fitbit.
 Unfortunately, the same can't be said for the distance metric, which calculates how far I ran. During the run, while glancing at my Google Fitbit Edge, it was consistently overestimating my running speed, often showing 30 seconds or more ahead of my Fenix, and that was reflected in the final distance result. While the Google Fitbit Edge said I ran 5.45 km , the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro measured just 5.15 km — a distance of around 300 meters.
 That's acceptable over a longer race, like a marathon (there was a similar discrepancy when I ran London with an Apple Watch and a Garmin ), but that's 300 meters over 42 kilometers, not five. 300 meters on this run equates to an overestimation of around 6%, and I trust the thousand-dollar Garmin's multi-band SatIQ GPS more than the sub-200-dollar Fitbit's.
 I will repeat the experiment with longer runs — with fewer trees — to see if I get a smaller deviation. It's not a dealbreaker for casual exercisers, but over 5% is enough for a keen runner to choose another device. Stay tuned for more testing and a full review of the Google Fitbit Edge very soon.

Should you buy the Luna Band?
 With the Oura Ring 5, Fitbit Edge, and Garmin Cirqa dominating this year’s fitness tracker new releases, I was extremely excited to test out the lesser-known Luna Band . A screen-free, subscription-free fitness tracker, the Luna Band certainly looks the part.
 But is looking the part enough to make it one of the best fitness trackers ? The TL;DR is this: at some point in the future, yes. 100%. The Luna Band has so much potential. But right now? It doesn’t feel finished. There are tons of “Coming Soon” banners in the app, and you can’t customize any personal targets — which is such a shame, because I genuinely adored testing it. I would recommend buying it, but not for a few months.
 I’ll get into all the gnarly details in this Luna Band review.

 Luna Band review: Price & availability 
 (Image credit: Tom's Guide) The Luna Band is $149 from Amazon U.S. and £129 direct from Luna in the U.K. This is $50 cheaper than the Garmin Cirqa and $50 cheaper than the Whoop 5.0 (from $199 to $369 per year ).
 However, the Fitbit Air ($99) and Amazfit Helio Strap ($99) both undercut the Luna Band by $50. The Luna Band looks much more appealing — and feels nicer on the skin — than the Amazfit Helio Strap and the silicone-y Fitbit Air strap (unless you pay extra for the upgraded knit option).
 Luna Band review: Design 
 (Image credit: Tom's Guide) The Luna Band looks fantastic. I have nothing bad to say about its appearance. I tested the beige option, but it also comes in black and green. You get two straps, S-M and M-L, which are between 240mm and 295mm long. There’s a decent amount of Velcro at one end, so you can tighten the strap to your preference. I have wrists that can only be described as “Victorian child”, and it fit me perfectly without looking weird.
 The Luna Band is also 5 ATM rated, which means you can wear it while swimming, but avoid high-impact water sports or scuba diving with it. I wore it in the ocean, and it both stayed put and didn’t get damaged.

 The fabric not only looks good, but it doesn’t trap heat or sweat, unlike the silicone wristband on my Apple Watch SE 3 .
 Luna Band review: Fitness features 
 (Image credit: Tom's Guide) The Luna Band offers a huge range of fitness tracking functions. However, you have to go into the “Health and Activity” tab of the Luna app to start a workout — it’s not on the home page (even though surely it should be?).
 Once I found the fitness section, I could scroll through 57 activities, although one of these is “Steam and Sauna Room,” not sure how “active” that one is. (To its credit, it does have a “Recovery” label next to it.)
 There’s no onboard GPS, so when you go for hikes, cycles, or runs, it won’t generate a nice map like Amazfit Helio Strap or Garmin Cirqa — even if you take your phone with you. This band feels more suited to general lifestyle use rather than conscious training programs.
 Automatic workout detection is a little blurry: I went for a run, but I clearly wasn’t running fast enough or long enough, as the Luna Band auto-detected a 4-minute run. This is a huge shame because my heart rate was between 144 and 162 BPM for thirty minutes on that day, but the band didn’t classify that as a run. There isn’t a huge amount of post-run analysis other than heart rate, so if you’re a serious runner, I’d recommend the Amazfit Helio Strap , Garmin Cirqa , or Fitbit Air instead.
 (Image credit: Tom's Guide) However, this is also an issue on the Amazfit Helio Strap. After these hiccups, I learned my lesson — and started a workout manually from the app every time. After workouts, you get a nice heart rate zone bar chart and cardio versus strength efficiency.
 I found the HRV to be somewhat unreliable. For a portion of my testing, I wore the Luna Band with my Amazfit Helio Strap, and the latter tracked my HRV at around 20 ms higher than the Luna Band. Of course, I can’t say for certain which was correct, but it’s worth mentioning.
 Some features, like blood oxygen, are grayed out with a “Coming Soon” badge. There are tons of “Coming Soon” graphics in the app — I joked to my colleagues that it looks like a “Coming Soon” wasteland.
 Unfortunately, I couldn’t test these “Coming Soon” areas. Does the blood oxygen saturation feature work? Who knows! For now, the Garmin Cirqa and Fitbit Air pip the Luna Band to the post here.
 Luna Band review: Extra features 
 The Luna app is replete with cool, lifestyle-oriented features. The home page has your ideal daily plan (but you can’t change it — more on that) and your peak score. Everything else shows up in the “Health” tab.
 Sleep tracking
 Sleep tracking on the Luna Band is one of its standout features. It tracks from the moment you lie down rather than when you fall asleep, so you can see your precise sleep latency. You don’t have to do math, like with the Amazfit Helio Strap, which tracks from the moment you fall asleep. Remembering what time I put my phone down when I’m groggy in the morning is always a challenge.
 Here’s a screenshot of an example night.
 (Image credit: Luna / Tom's Guide) I love seeing the stratification of my sleep quality and my body’s response during the night. Tracking HRV is one of the most important things I look for in a fitness tracker.
 However — and I’ll get into this in more detail in the “App” section — you can’t adjust your sleep targets. I don’t want my sleep target to be 7 hours; I want it to be 8 hours. You can’t change this because the band works out how much sleep it thinks I need. But I don’t care how much sleep the fitness tracker thinks I need — I want my target to be how much sleep I think I need. I checked with the built-in chatbot, and it told me you can’t customize these targets manually.
 Peak score
 At first, I hoped Peak Score would be more like Amazfit’s BioCharge feature, but it doesn’t really work like that. While BioCharge goes down during the day and resets at night, Peak Score uses your workout data, sleep data, and general wellbeing data to generate a set daily number. This means if you run a marathon, your peak score won’t change.
 While this isn’t inherently wrong or bad, it’s worth noting if you’d like a dynamic number that reflects your activity for the day. For example, if you run in the morning and go to a boxing class in the evening and want to know how hard you can push yourself.
 I like Peak Score, and I like Amazfit’s BioCharge. Both have their merits.
 Luna Band review: App 
 (Image credit: Tom's Guide) The Luna app is less fitness-focused and more lifestyle-oriented. While it does still offer insights into energy, readiness, and so on, it also features tons of suggestions for eating, walking, and sleeping,
 My prevailing thought regarding the app is that I wish Luna hadn’t released it unfinished. Because that’s what it is — unfinished. The app wants you to sleep for seven hours; walk 5,000 steps; burn 410 active calories; walk/run 8km a day. There’s no option to change any of these targets, or, if there is, it’s incredibly well-hidden — and the built-in AI chatbot doesn’t know how to change it either.
 That brings me to my next point: there is, however, an AI chatbot in the app, because of course there is! I wish the Luna team had spent more time finishing the app — allowing you to actually set personal targets — rather than polishing said AI chatbot.
 (Image credit: Luna / Tom's Guide) I don’t want to sleep for seven hours; I want to sleep for eight. I don’t want to walk 5,000 steps; I want to walk 10,000. Sure, you can do this manually, but I want the dopamine release of the app itself congratulating me for reaching my more difficult target.
 It’s really unfortunate, because the app itself is beautifully laid out. The design team has done a great job. Everything is sleek, well-designed, and easy to understand. At first, I wondered if the app could do with more easily navigable customization tabs, but then I realised there were none. Again — a huge shame, because the Luna Band has serious potential.
 However, there’s no subscription, which is a huge plus over Whoop, which requires a subscription, and the Fitbit Air and Garmin Cirqa, which lock some features behind a monthly paywall. Even so, I would recommend waiting for these “Coming Soon” features to actually arrive.
 Luna Band review: Battery life 
 (Image credit: Tom's Guide) The Luna Band is rated for around 10 days. I found this accurate during testing — I charged it four times over a five-week period.
 This battery life isn’t as good as the Whoop 5.0 (14 days) or Amazfit Helio Strap (14 days), but it’s better than the Fitbit Air (one week) and equals the Garmin Cirqa. I’m extremely happy with this battery life.
 Should you buy the Luna Band? 
 (Image credit: Tom's Guide) Right now? No. I’d recommend waiting until the app is actually finished. There’s little point in investing in a new fitness tracker and learning the app when there’s actually not that much to learn right now.
 This is such a shame, because I really enjoyed using the Luna Band. It’s sleek, pretty, inconspicuous. It’s much smaller and more feminine than the Amazfit Helio Strap, and cheaper than the Garmin Cirqa. On top of that, there’s no subscription, which is amazing.
 Choosing the Luna Band’s rating was incredibly hard because I genuinely loved wearing this fitness tracker. Sleep tracking is fantastic. The app design is gorgeous. It’s just a shame Luna released it before it was ready.

The best watch for a marathon runner won't necessarily suit someone who just wants to move more, and the priciest model isn't automatically the smartest buy.

 Frequently Asked Questions 
 What's the best smartwatch for women?
 We've got a more detailed entry on this topic below , but in short, for the most part there are no major differences between smartwatches for women and men.
 That said, size may be a favor here, so you may prefer to look for a model that's designed for smaller wrists, such as Garmin's Lily range. 
 Some smartwatches also provide features specific to women's health, although in other cases these are options available within the platform you're using and are not restricted to particular models; Apple Watch Series 8 or later, including the Series 11 and Apple Watch Ultra models...
 How do you charge a smartwatch?
 Unlike smartphones, most smartwatches tend to use a proprietary charger, often a magnetic one. Though they are always included with the watch, this can be frustrating if you lose yours or it breaks. 
 Some chargers will work for multiple models – for instance many Garmins and most Apple Watches are capable of using the same charger, although some older chargers may not be as fast as newer ones. Some can also be charged wirelessly either using Wireless PowerShare from a phone or the Qi standard; check your specific model for details. 
 Which model you use, you should generally remove it from the charger once it’s full; though most devices will have built-in safety features to prevent overcharging, leaving your watch on charge for too long could still degrade the device's lithium-ion battery over time.
 How to set the time on a smartwatch
 Unlike with a non-smart watch, setting the time on a smartwatch is simply a matter of syncing the device to your phone via Bluetooth, using the relevant app. The smartwatch will then take the time from the phone.
 What's the best military smartwatch?
 Several of the best rugged smartwatches are also good choices for military use, and you can also buy plenty of non-smart watches from the likes of Casio that have many useful features for the military including top-notch weatherproofing, long battery life, night-vision backlighting and more. 
 Focusing solely on smart models, Garmin offers a range of ‘Tactical Edition’ watches with ‘stealth’ mode, ballistics information (like a compass/golf watch, that takes wind and weapon range into account) and a quick-wipe ‘kill switch’.
 How does a smartwatch measure sleep?
 Smartwatches are a great way to track the duration and quality of your sleep. Whatever the model, a smartwatch will use heart-rate variability information and motion detection to estimate sleep stages and quality – with varying degrees of accuracy.
 Some smartwatches, such as the Samsung Galaxy Watch 9 and the latest Apple Watch models, including the Series 11 and Ultra 3, even have advanced features such as sleep apnea detection.
 How do you set up a smartwatch?
 How you set up your smartwatch will depend on which model you have, but all will follow a roughly similar process.
 In almost all cases you'll follow instructions to sync the smartwatch to your phone – either by scanning the watch with your phone’s camera if using an Apple Watch, or by downloading an app – and will then follow instructions from there.
 Every smartwatch will have its own app, whether Garmin, Pixel, Apple, Polar, Amazfit or any others.
 How to choose the best smartwatch for you 
 Unfortunately, your choice of smartwatch often depends on your choice of phone, as not all wearables are compatible with competitor devices. Apple Watch only works with Apple iPhones. Samsung and Google watches, and other Wear OS devices, only work with Android devices, but you can use a Samsung watch with a Google phone and vice versa.
 Dedicated fitness watches from Garmin, Coros and Polar generally offer much longer battery life than Wear OS or Apple watches, often lasting a week or more between charges. If training is your priority, they're worth considering even if they don't offer the same app ecosystem.
 Most wearables will get about a day of battery life, which will be disappointing if you're converting from a Garmin watch that lasts weeks. You can find a few watches that last longer on this list.
 Finally, smartwatches can be expensive, and frankly, they don't offer much value for what you pay. Before you spring for an Apple Watch Ultra, you might ask if you are really going Scuba diving this year, or if you're just going to check your text messages without disturbing your dinner mates.
 The best smartwatch for women vs men: Is there a difference?
 There are no specific differences when it comes to smartwatches for women or men, and choosing the right one usually comes down to personal preference. 
 One of the main considerations is making sure the watch size fits your wrist. Many smartwatches are quite large, which can feel bulky on slimmer wrists, so it’s worth checking the case size before buying. Many models come in multiple sizes, and when that’s the case, we list the options in our full reviews to help you choose the best fit.
 Some smartwatches also include features focused on women's health. These can include menstrual cycle tracking, ovulation predictions, and symptom logging, often powered by data such as heart rate trends, sleep patterns, and skin temperature. These tools can help provide a broader picture of hormonal cycles and overall well-being.
 This doesn't mean those watches are only designed for women, nor that these features must be used. Most are optional and can be enabled or ignored depending on your preferences.
 If you do plan to use them, it's worth checking the privacy policy of the watch you've bought so you understand where your health data is stored and who can access it.
 Can you use Apple Watch with an Android phone?
 The first thing to check is whether your phone is compatible with the smartwatch you want. You can't use an Apple Watch with an Android phone, as all the functions of watchOS require iOS to interface with. 
 You can't use an Apple Watch with an Android phone, as Apple Watch requires an iPhone for setup and everyday use.
 Likewise, Google Pixel Watch and Samsung Galaxy Watch models are designed for Android phones and don't support iPhone. If you regularly switch between Android and iOS, a Garmin, Amazfit or CMF smartwatch is usually a better choice because these work with both platforms.
 How we test smartwatches 
 Every smartwatch on this list has been fully and extensively reviewed by the expert team at TechRadar, so we know exactly what makes them tick.
 Our review process involves using the devices as if they were our own personal wearables, ensuring every smartwatch gets fully tested in the real world. A comprehensive sweep of features takes place, and usage is varied over a week to give us a clear idea of how battery life performs.
 When testing in-house, we generally look at how accurate the GPS is on each smartwatch by testing it against an industry leader such as the Garmin Epix Pro . Likewise for workout metrics. We also rank how usable the watch's operating system is, whether it supports third-party apps, and where it sits in the market. For example, a cheap watch with fewer features is more likely to get four stars than a feature-stuffed premium watch that isn't worth the expensive price.
 Using that knowledge we've then ranked them, factoring in their value, design, features, and performance to get an overall star verdict.

 If one of your health goals is to lose weight, wearing a fitness tracker, including one of the best Apple Watches , is a great place to start. To lose weight and keep it off, you’ll need to ensure you’re burning more calories than you consume — otherwise known as a calorie deficit.
 One of the easiest ways to see how many calories you’re burning is to wear a fitness tracker. Yet, if you’ve got an Apple Watch on your wrist, how you set up your watch can make all the difference. Read on to find out more.
 As a reminder, if you’re looking for personalized advice when it comes to weight loss, it’s always a good idea to talk to your physician.
 Latest Videos From Tom's Guide 
 Watch full video here: 
 How to set up your Apple Watch for weight loss 
 Whether you choose the Apple Watch SE 3 , the Apple Watch Series 12 , or invest in the Apple Watch Ultra 4 , there are a few ways to ensure your watch gives you the most accurate health data. Here are three top tips:
 1. Get the fit right 
 (Image credit: Future) Let’s caveat something here: no smartwatch or sports watch on the market will be 100% accurate when it comes to estimating how many calories you’ve actually burned. They largely rely on algorithms, and to really get an idea of your true energy expenditure every day, you’d need to be wired up in a lab.
 You may like

 I walked another 8,000 steps with the Apple Watch 12 and Fitbit Edge: Here’s which came out on top 
 That said, your Apple Watch will estimate your calorie expenditure using your heart rate data, as well as your personal metrics, plus data from the movement sensors and GPS. How accurately your watch records all of this data depends on how well it fits.
 Your Apple Watch should be snug, not tight, with the heart rate sensor sitting flush against your wrist. The watch should sit above your wrist bone, and it shouldn’t be loose enough to rotate as you move.

 2. Make sure your settings are correct and your watch is calibrated 
 Remember those personal metrics I just mentioned that form part of the calorie expenditure algorithm on your Apple Watch? It’s important to make sure these are accurate, especially as you start losing weight, because they can make a big difference.
 (Image credit: Future) It’s also important to ensure that your Apple Watch is calibrated, as this makes the data more accurate. Firstly, head to Location Services on your iPhone, click System Services , then Motion Calibration and Distance and make sure it’s turned on. Next, go for a 20-minute walk in a flat area where you can see clear blue skies (heavily wooded areas or skyscrapers can affect GPS) at your natural pace wearing the Apple Watch, as this will make sure it’s calibrated to your stride.
 3. Choose the right workout mode 
 Finally, another important step when it comes to getting the most accurate idea of your calorie expenditure is to choose the right workout mode on your Apple Watch. Each workout type will use a specialized algorithm tailored to the expected movement pattern.
 (Image credit: Future) For example, I’d often use Functional Strength Training mode during my HIIT workouts in the gym. When I switched to using High-Intensity Interval Training, my average calorie burn was higher. This is because the Apple Watch is weighing the elevated heart rate that comes with a HIIT session with short periods of rest more heavily than it would in strength training mode.
 Of course, even when your watch is set up perfectly, it’s important to reiterate again that no wearable will be perfect when it comes to estimating your overall calorie expenditure. The best way to lose weight is to eat a balanced, healthy diet, prioritize movement, and focus on your overall health.

 Zwift and TrainerRoad are two indoor cycling apps which take very different approaches to improving your cycling performance .
 Zwift offers you a virtual world in which to ride and the option to interact with other riders on the platform.
 TrainerRoad is purely focused on your own objectives and scheduling the workouts to achieve them. Its user interface is graph-based and will suit those focused on the data and process.
 Latest Videos From Cyclingnews 
 Watch full video here: 
 Just this week, Zwift launched a new premium subscription tier called Zwift Plus. The package costs around $10 more and adds adaptive AI coaching and real-world video.
 The two apps are likely to appeal to very different riders and mental outlooks. Which is right for you? We’ll help you understand what Zwift and TrainerRoad offer and choose the platform that suits you best.
 You may like

 Zwift vs TrainerRoad: Approach
 Zwift's gamified environment offers the option to ride with or against others (Image credit: Zwift) Zwift may have retired its “fun is fast” mantra, but it still aims to provide a varied approach to training, offering freeriding and racing, as well as more structured training plans and workouts.
 TrainerRoad is much more objective-focused, claiming it will “make you faster with science-based, goal-driven training”. That goal-driven approach is key to the app’s appeal. If you’re training for a race or a challenge, TrainerRoad will set out a plan of workouts that’s claimed to help you to prepare. There's no in-game or social element; it's all about the training.

 The latest race content, interviews, features, reviews and expert buying guides, direct to your inbox!
 Zwift vs TrainerRoad: Adaptive training 
 TrainerRoad presents your workout as a series of ramps (Image credit: Josh Ross) TrainerRoad’s selling point is its adaptive training. It offers both targeted training and a Train Now option.
 While targeted Custom Plans are structured and power-based, Train Now is more flexible and proposes workouts based on your fitness level. Train Now also lets you flex your schedule if you’re time-pressed, or just want to add in some unstructured indoor or outdoor riding.
 There’s a large library of workouts and TrainerRoad will suggest an appropriate next workout based on your objectives, fitness and recovery status. Based on your performance during a workout, the app will assess your “Progression Level” and fine-tune your schedule.
 What to read next
 The indoor cycling app scene is evolving, so what options are currently out there and do they challenge Zwift's dominance? 
 Types of indoor bike trainer explained, and which should you choose? 
 Get 10% off the Zwift Ride V2 bundle, and gear up for indoor riding with the ultimate Zwift indoor cycling setup 
 Zwift too has a large library of structured training plans , focused on different aspects of performance, such as boosting your FTP or increasing your endurance. Its plans don’t include any flexibility – miss a workout, and it won’t be rescheduled for you. There are short-duration workouts for the time-pressed as well as longer options.
 Zwift also has a partnership with TrainerRoad, which allows you to add in a structured schedule and annual plan that you can ride in Zwift. This does mean paying for two separate subscriptions, though.
 The new Zwift Plus coaching offering builds on what the platform already offers. The new Zwift Coach promises to set a goal, analyse performance and adapt over time.
 Zwift vs TrainerRoad: Objective setting
 TrainerRoad's forte is its adaptive training (Image credit: Trainerroad) Progression Levels in TrainerRoad are assessed across seven aspects, from sprint power to endurance capacity. TrainerRoad suggests that your performance across these dimensions can change without a change in your FTP, so this will again feed into its future workout recommendations.
 TrainerRoad also offers a large amount of sports science-based advice to help you to understand the scientific basis of performance and how to improve.
 Zwift’s workouts tend to focus on one aspect of your fitness. It’s up to you to decide what this is and choose a training plan to match, and there’s limited feedback. Its workouts are based around your FTP, which you can either measure via an FTP test there are a few options to choose from or input directly if you know it, or rely on Zwift’s assessment based on your previous riding.
 Zwift vs TrainerRoad: Competition
 Zwift’s offer is geared around riding with others. With over a million active users worldwide, you can find others riding in its worlds day and night, and there are events scheduled both by Zwift and its user base, allowing you to ride with or race against other riders.
 You can also add “Robopacers” to set a tempo to encourage you to keep up. The gamified aspect is epitomised by Zwift’s PowerUps, which allow you to increase your in-game performance briefly.
 TrainerRoad is much more straight-laced and just focuses on your training. There’s no interactivity with other users and little visual stimulation. If you don't want or need to interact with other riders, and want to jump on to complete a structured session, TrainerRoad may suit you more.
 Zwift vs TrainerRoad: User interface
 Zwift adds new roads to keep its interface interesting (Image credit: Zwift) Zwift’s training is based in its virtual worlds, with the app showing you an imaginary road complete with volcanoes, banners, other riders and more. It will interact with your smart trainer to increase resistance when the virtual road’s gradient increases and ease off when you’re on the flat or descending.
 TrainerRoad, meanwhile, takes a more traditional training approach, displaying a series of graph-like ramps where ride intensity increases and decreases. You can follow this on a non-smart trainer as well as with automatic resistance changes using a smart trainer. It’s probably less engaging for most riders, but it allows you to focus more on what’s coming up and meeting the power demands of your workout or to watch or listen to something of your choice.
 Zwift vs TrainerRoad: Hardware
 There's a range of Zwift-ready hardware to help you get started on the platform (Image credit: Zwift) While you can run Zwift on pretty much any hardware, the brand works with smart trainer makers to sell Zwift Ready equipment, designed to make setup faster, as well as its own brand Zwift Ride 2 indoor bike with or without a Wahoo Kickr Core 2 trainer.
 There’s an increasing range of Zwift Ready trainers that come ready-fitted with Zwift’s orange single sprocket Cog and are packaged with its Click bar-mounted shifters. These do tie you into using Zwift or Rouvy , which Zwift also owns.
 In contrast, TrainerRoad is trainer-agnostic and doesn’t sell branded hardware. It has detailed information on compatible non-smart and smart trainers and online and in-person help to get set up.
 Zwift vs TrainerRoad: Price
 Zwift is priced at £17.99 a month, although an annual subscription reduces that to £15 equivalent. There’s a 30-day money-back period for annual subscribers, whereas monthly subscribers get a 14-day free trial period before they’re billed.
 The new Zwit Plus package costs £26.99 / €29.99 / $29.99 per month. There are also yearly discounts to take advantage of if you want to pay in one go.
 TrainerRoad bills exclusively in US dollars, with an annual membership costing $209.99 or $17.45 monthly equivalent, while paying monthly raises this to $21.99 per month. In both cases, there’s a 30-day money-back period.
 Zwift vs TrainerRoad: Which should you choose?
 Zwift and TrainerRoad’s very different user experiences will appeal to different riders and different motivations.
 If you’re very goal-focused and like to plan out your training in advance, maybe targeting a specific event or schedule of events during your riding year, TrainerRoad will support you. It's all about the work, but it still offers some flexibility and will adapt to your schedule and progression, and assesses your progress across a range of aspects of your fitness, not just FTP.
 If, on the other hand, you like the element of competition when training, value the visual stimulation of its virtual world and its gamified, more engaging user interface, Zwift is more likely to keep your interest level up and help you achieve your goals. Plus, there’s the option to use Zwift to support your structured training on TrainerRoad.

He also notes that they're great at reminding you to do daily health tasks like drinking water, "which is essential to performance and assists in normalizing blood pressure."
 Overall, they're a great tool for tracking fitness data. But the real question is: Which one is right for you? With so many high-tech features, shopping for one can be almost as confusing as shopping for walking shoes , an under-desk treadmill , or a weighted vest . That's why our team of Women's Health editors and in-house fitness enthusiasts put a handful to the test to help you figure out which tracker is best for certain goals. The price also includes a six-month membership to Fitbit Premium, which features a library of cardio and strength training workouts and a monthly analysis of 10 sleep metrics. The Charge 2 was my first ever fitness tracker, so I have a soft spot for the Charge line. Instead of manually recording workouts, it automatically records movement such as walking, swimming, and biking, which is nice instead of fiddling around with a watch interface (although it's a simple swipe). Speaking of swimming, the tracker can be submerged in water up to 50 meters, so I never have to take it off when showering.
 It has a sensor on the back of the slim rectangular watch case to track heart rate, which never disrupts my range of motion during weight lifting or mat Pilates. When comparing against higher-end models like the Garmin Vivoactive, my heart rate data matched up, which proves its lower price tag doesn't equal lower quality. Aside from heart rate, it also tracks stress levels, period, fertility insights, and sleep.
 I'm not a fan of wearing a watch to bed, but this model is so lightweight (30 grams) and thin that I barely notice it. It provides a sleep score breakdown of all your sleep cycles and whether or not your sleep was optimal for recovery, which is especially helpful if you're in the process of training for a race or going hard at the gym. It also records your sleep duration, but I found it recognizes sedentary activities such as watching TV as sleeping, which got on my nerves slightly. Post-snooze, it delivers a personalized daily readiness score, which shows if you're ready for a sweat sesh.
 It pairs perfectly with Android smartphones, given that Google owns Fitbit (a Google account is also required to set up). It seamlessly interacts with calendar and weather apps, plus you can receive texts, notifications, calls, and access Spotify. Fitbit Pay is built in, too, for easy access to cardless payments.
 The biggest con with the Charge 6 is that the battery drains fast. Fitbit says it lasts up to a week, but I found it needs to be charged by day four. It's not a huge deal, just make sure to carry a charger if you're traveling. As for the warranty, it lasts one year and provides coverage in the event the hardware is defective, so make sure you don't lose it.

 What to Consider
 Heart rate monitor
 Nelson says the most important feature of any fitness tracker is a good heart rate monitor, whether you’re a hardcore athlete or a workout noob. “This feature can be used to dictate the rate of perceived exertion (RPE), which is important for exercise intensity," Nelson says. "Identifying your resting heart rate is important as it’s a marker of cardiovascular fitness because it can give you a better sense of what your maximal heart rate is, which would be more accurate than using prediction formulas." While a fitness tracker isn’t as accurate as a chest strap, it still provides a good look at your exertion levels for moderate to intense activities, according to a 2019 study by Cardiovascular Diagnosis & Therapy .
 Sleep tracking
 Nelson also likes to track his sleep with a fitness tracker, since sleep is the main way our bodies recover. Being aware of your sleep habits and behaviors can shed light on how you feel the next day. For context, most trackers analyze sleep cycles, trends, and needs.
 Size and weight
 Weight might not seem like a big deal, but when you're wearing your fitness tracker all day, a heftier model becomes a lot more noticeable than you'd expect. There is no best size when it comes to fitness trackers, as it comes down to the types of activities you're most likely to use yours for. For outdoor enthusiasts into running , hiking, and trail running , we suggest prioritizing durability over a minimalist design. If you're looking for a fitness tracker for everyday wear, walking , strength training , or mostly indoor activities, you might appreciate a lightweight design. But, of course, it all comes down to personal preference and what feels best for your wrist size.
 Battery life
 Many of the best fitness trackers can run for days or even weeks on a single charge, such as the Garmin Vivoactive. Charging every day can be a nuisance, which is why most of the fitness trackers we recommend have a solid battery life of at least a few days. But battery doesn't always equate to quality, given that something like the Apple Watch Series 11 needs to be charged every day for optimal use, and it’s still one of our absolute favorites.
 Ease of use
 As with all tech, you want a fitness tracker that's easy to use. For Ellis, this is among the top three most important considerations, and it makes sense. If your new tracker isn't intuitive to set up or use daily, you're far less likely to use it consistently. Ultimately, the only way to know for sure is to try it out yourself to see if it works for you. That's another reason why it's smart to buy a fitness tracker with a generous return policy.
 How We Selected
 I, along with other Women’s Health and Men’s Health editors, have tested dozens of the latest fitness trackers over the last year while running, walking, strength training, hiking, and just during everyday life. We compared every feature and spec, from durability and wearability to features and accuracy. Additionally, we also consulted with fitness experts Ellis and Nelson to get their professional opinions on why you should buy a fitness tracker and what to look out for. Whether you’re an athlete serious about training or seeking one for daily recreational use, there’s definitely a model we tested that fits your needs.
 Meet the Experts
 N’Namdi Nelson , CSCS , is an exercise physiologist at the NYU Langone Sports Performance Center .
 Almoni Ellis , CPT, CES, PPSC, is an exercise science professional based in Virginia.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Are the best fitness trackers accurate for tracking vital health metrics?
 Based on his research, Nelson says that wrist-based fitness trackers are “relatively accurate in measuring number of steps, distance, sleep duration, and heart rate.” One caveat, however, is that they tend to overestimate total energy expenditure during low-intensity aerobic workouts and underestimate it during high-intensity workouts. For the most accurate measurements, it’s best to consult with a fitness professional.
 What’s the most accurate fitness tracker?
 Based on his research, Nelson says that wrist-based fitness trackers are "relatively accurate in measuring number of steps, distance, sleep duration, and heart rate." One caveat, however, is that they tend to overestimate total energy expenditure during low-intensity aerobic workouts and underestimate it during high-intensity workouts. For the most accurate measurements, it's best to consult with a fitness professional.
 For sleep tracking though, we’d argue a ring, like the Oura Ring 4, is most accurate. It sits most snugly to your skin, which is particularly important for sleep metrics.
 Should I buy a fitness tracker?
 If you're curious about what's happening with your body throughout the day (how well you slept, how hard your heart is working during a workout, whether you're recovering enough between training sessions, or why your energy tanks every afternoon) a fitness tracker is worth the investment. You don't need to be a competitive athlete to benefit from one. Even casual gym-goers, walkers, and people focused on improving their sleep can use the data for accountability and forming solid wellness habits.
 That said, a fitness tracker isn't a medical device, and the data should be used as a general guide rather than a diagnosis. If you find yourself obsessing over every metric or losing sleep over a low readiness score, it might do more harm than good. Your best bet is to use the data as just one bit of info next to actual real-life evidence—like how you feel, how you're performing, what your healthcare provider recommends, and what your own goals look like. For most people, though, the awareness alone is worth it.

Fitness trackers are a convenient way for health-minded people to track various stats, set goals, and monitor their progress. In addition to workout metrics, a device can help you accurately track sleep, body temperature, hydration, and more. According to personal trainer Kira Jones, CPT, the main benefit of wearing a fitness tracker is that it provides tangible data about your fitness and overall health.

To find the best fitness trackers, we first spoke with two fitness experts to determine which key features to look for in high-quality options. Then, we spent over one year testing 36 of the most popular devices, using them while we worked out, slept, and went about our everyday routines for over a month. We evaluated each one for its ease of setup, comfort, ease of use, accuracy, connectivity, features, and value to find the top options on the market.

Plus, we didn’t have to charge it every day or worry about running out of juice mid-workout, thanks to its 60-hour battery life.

Potential Flaws
People with smaller wrists or those who sleep with their wrists bent may find the watch uncomfortable to wear overnight.
Users who prefer a personalized dashboard may find the watch less flexible than competing fitness trackers.

Fitness Trackers and Watches We Also Tested

We spent over one year testing 36 fitness trackers, but only 14 earned a spot on our final list of recommendations. Although these options didn't score high enough to make the final cut, we still think they have some features worth mentioning.

FITVII’s Health & Fitness Tracker is a budget-friendly option that accurately tracks basic metrics like steps and heart rate. However, during testing, it felt a bit bulky, and we found that some of its features, such as cycle tracking, didn’t work properly.
Although we found Fitbit’s Charge 6 to be very comfortable and accurate for sleep tracking, we had trouble using the built-in GPS and syncing workouts with third-party apps.
Casio’s G-SHOCK DWH5600 has a rugged design and providesƒ accurate metrics for steps and heart rate during testing. However, it lacks convenient features such as automatic activity detection. We also found the setup process and interface to be very nonintuitive.
 When testing Samsung’s Galaxy Watch 7, we found it easy to set up, customize, and integrate with our smartphone. However, the band felt bulky, and we were disappointed that the auto-stop feature was unreliable.
Amazfit’s Helio Ring is more budget-friendly than other smart rings, and we were impressed with its comfortable, discreet design and sleep-tracking accuracy. However, we found its workout tracking and activity metrics to be somewhat limited.
We tested 35 fitness trackers in a variety of conditions.

Verywell Fit

What We’ve Updated
Since publishing our tested roundup of the best fitness trackers, we’ve re-evaluated our previous picks and hands-on tested eight new devices. We evaluated each device for its ease of setup, ease of use, comfort, connectivity, features, accuracy, and value to find the top options on the market.
Based on long-term testing and our most recent testing insights, we’ve reworked our product picks for some of our superlatives, including Best Smart Watch for Sleep, Best Ring, and more. We’ve also added new superlatives, including Best Fitness Tracker for Everyday Use and Most Comfortable Fitness Watch.
Types of Fitness Trackers and Watches

Fitness trackers come in all shapes and sizes, and you’ll want to choose one that feels comfortable and best meets your needs. These are the types we recommend, and the most common ones you’ll come across while shopping.

Smartwatch: A smartwatch is essentially an extension of your smartphone on your wrist, providing convenient access to apps, alerts, notifications, calls, music, and more. Although they don’t always offer the same robust data and analysis as fitness wristbands, they can still track metrics like daily steps and heart rate, as well as workout data such as distance, pace, and elevation, using GPS.
Fitness Wristbands: These devices tend to be smaller, lighter, and more comfortable than smartwatches, making them a better option for all-day wear and sleep tracking. Beginner exercisers and less tech-savvy people also like that they’re usually budget-friendly and easy to use. However, they may not have built-in GPS or offer the same integration with your phone as a smartwatch.
Smart Rings: A smart ring is a subtle, wearable tracker that doubles as a piece of jewelry and monitors metrics such as sleep, daily activity, body temperature, and stress. They’re usually comfortable to wear all day and to bed, and typically offer comprehensive sleep, heart rate, and stress tracking. However, smart rings’ workout tracking capabilities are not always as accurate as wrist-worn models, and some require a monthly subscription to access all your data.  
Armbands: Although not as popular as other types, armbands are especially good for accurately tracking your heart rate. They’re very comfortable for distance runs or rides, but aren’t the most suitable option for everyday wear.
A smart ring can be worn on a finger just like jewelry.

Verywell Fit

What to Look for When Shopping for Fitness Trackers and Watches
Metrics and Health Features: Start by deciding what you want to track. Most fitness trackers cover the basics, including steps, heart rate, distance, calories burned, and sleep. If you're training for a race, monitoring recovery, or tracking specific health metrics, you may want advanced features like GPS, heart rate variability (HRV), blood oxygen monitoring, training readiness scores, or workout-specific tracking.
Comfort and Wearability: The best fitness tracker is the one you'll actually wear. Since many people wear their trackers all day and night, a comfortable fit, lightweight design, and a display that's easy to read at a glance are all important. Some models also offer interchangeable bands if you want a device that can transition from workouts to everyday wear.
Battery Life: Battery life can vary from a few days to several weeks, depending on the device and the features you use. Always-on displays, GPS tracking, and frequent notifications tend to drain the battery faster. If you don't want to charge your tracker often, prioritize models with longer battery life.
Compatibility and Smart Features: Most fitness trackers sync with smartphones, but compatibility can vary by operating system and app ecosystem. Before buying, make sure your tracker works with your phone and any fitness apps you already use. Some devices also offer extras like music controls, contactless payments, and call or text notifications.
Water Resistance and Durability: If you plan to swim or exercise outdoors, pay attention to the device's water-resistance rating and overall durability. Many fitness trackers are suitable for pool swimming, but not all are designed for open-water activities or frequent exposure to the elements.
Price: More expensive fitness trackers often include advanced training tools, health insights, built-in GPS, and smartwatch features. If you only want to track daily activity, sleep, and heart rate, a budget-friendly option may be all you need.
When choosing a fitness tracker and watch, consider the style, metrics, and battery life.

Verywell Fit

How We Tested the Fitness Trackers

Fitness trackers work best when used over the long term, allowing them to adapt to your lifestyle. For the most precise testing results, we spent over one year testing 36 fitness trackers at home during a one-month period, wearing them while working out, sleeping, and in our daily routines. When testing fitness trackers and watches, we evaluate each option based on the following key criteria.

Ease of Setup: After unboxing the new fitness trackers, we set them up and assess how intuitive the process is. We note if we encounter any issues or difficulties during the setup. We also determine if there are any features or functions that are particularly difficult to understand or use.
Comfort: We wear each tracker for a variety of workouts and for several hours throughout our day. We note if the strap or sensor feels secure and comfortable on our skin or if it causes irritation. We consider things like: Does the strap have enough adjustability? Is it sleek and lightweight or bulky and cumbersome? Is it sweatproof? Is it comfy to sleep with it on? Since a fitness tracker is only effective if worn regularly, we prioritize comfortable trackers.
Ease of Use: As we test the device, we note the difficulty level of tracking workouts and accessing data. If there's an app, we also note how easy it is to navigate and whether graphics and other details are clear and easy to understand. We take note of whether the metrics are useful and how simple it is to customize the settings. We also assess how responsive the touchscreen or control interface is to use.
Accuracy: In addition to evaluating the tracker’s precision, we also note how quickly its monitor responds to changes in our heart rate during a workout. We check how easily it detects different types of movement, for example, walking versus running. If we have other means of tracking metrics, such as another fitness tracker, our phone, or a heart rate monitor, we compare the data from these other trackers to the device we’re testing.
Features: As we continue to test the tracker, we evaluate the range and quality of its health and fitness tracking and analysis. We also take note of gamification, motivation, and goal-setting features that encourage consistent use. We consider whether the tracker offers personalized features based on data and user preferences, such as training plans or customized displays. We also check if the watch has mental health elements, such as stress monitoring or mindfulness support.
Connectivity: To evaluate the connectivity of each device, we evaluate whether the tracker syncs seamlessly with our smartphone or other devices. We consider whether notifications are delivered in real-time and are accurate. We also make note of any dropped signals or syncing issues.
Value: We thoroughly test each fitness tracker without knowing its cost, and only check the price at the end of our testing period. We then determine the value score based on whether the price accurately reflects the features and quality, and our experience with the device. We think critically about whether we would buy the item at its current price and if we would recommend it to friends and family members.
Testers evaluated each watch and fitness tracker for comfort, connectivity, and ease of use.

Verywell Fit

Our Experts

We consulted experts at each stage of our research, testing, and reporting process. The following experts helped us better understand what key features to look for when shopping for a high-quality option and potential flaws to be aware of. We also asked about specific fitness trackers they would recommend and took their input into account when choosing which trackers to test. While we select products independently, expert input helps inform our decisions.

Kira Jones, CPT, personal trainer and founder of Cacti Wellness Collective in New York City
Noelle McKenzie, ACE-CPT, personal trainer and co-founder of Leading Edge Personal Trainers in New York City
Frequently Asked Questions
What is the best fitness tracker overall?

During our testing, we found all of our picks to be accurate and high-performing. Our favorite overall fitness tracker is the Garmin vívosmart 5 thanks to its comfortable, lightweight design, intuitive interface, and ability to accurately track a wide range of activities, including HIIT workouts, treadmill runs, hikes, and sleep. We also love its seamless integration with the Garmin Connect app, which provides detailed insights, personalized metrics, and motivating challenges that make it easier to understand and improve your health and fitness habits.

Is it worth it to buy a smartwatch for exercise tracking?

For many people, yes. Features like GPS, heart rate tracking, workout-specific modes, sleep monitoring, and recovery metrics can provide valuable insights into your fitness routine. A smartwatch is often the best choice if you also want notifications, music controls, navigation, and other everyday conveniences. If your primary goal is simply tracking steps, workouts, sleep, and heart rate, a fitness band may provide everything you need at a lower price. Smart rings are another good option for people who prioritize comfort and passive health tracking over workout features.

What are the benefits of using a fitness tracker? 

Fitness trackers support physical and mental well-being by helping users stay accountable to their goals, says McKenzie. By tracking activity, sleep, heart rate, and other health metrics, they can provide motivation and encourage more movement throughout the day. They can also help identify patterns over time, making it easier to adjust your habits and monitor progress. Whether you choose a band, smartwatch, or smart ring, the best fitness tracker is one you'll wear consistently.

How long does a fitness tracker last?

Higher-end fitness trackers and smartwatches can often last five years or more with proper care, while budget-friendly models may show signs of wear after two to three years. Components such as straps and batteries are sometimes replaceable, which can extend the life of the device. If longevity is a priority, smartwatches and premium fitness bands tend to offer the best value over time, while smart rings may require more frequent battery replacement or charging due to their compact size.

Why Trust Verywell Fit

Jen Zeltwanger, ACSM-EP, is an ACSM-certified exercise physiologist and Verywell Fit writer. She has lots of experience with in-home and outdoor fitness and tracks it all wearing an Apple Watch. Jen knows what works and what to look for when shopping for fitness products, and she prioritizes products that are easy to use, versatile, and of high quality.

Additional reporting contributed by Christine Luff, ACE-CPT

A certified personal trainer, running coach, gym buff, and Verywell Fit writer, Christine Luff, ACE-CPT, spends countless hours researching and testing the latest exercise gear and gadgets. She consistently wears an Apple Watch to track her outdoor runs, daily steps, and other health and fitness data.

Both authors reviewed testing insights to help create this list of top performers.

 How we test fitness trackers and watches for women
 Our fitness tracker and watch reviews are based on tests in the Tech & Engineering Lab. In the past two years, our analysts and engineers have evaluated more than 30 different fitness trackers and watches . 
 Isabella Cavallo / Good Housekeeping Institute 
 Lipski, our senior reviews writer and analyst, test engineers, and I have each used a handful of fitness trackers and smart watches. I tried five fitness trackers at home, while Lipski has tested all the latest Apple Watch models, including Series 10 and 11. Some trackers were also given to consumer testers, who provided qualitative feedback that called out specific features they appreciated, like a watch's sleep score or reminders to stand and stretch throughout the day.
 Most of our testing involved assessing how the fitness trackers performed during real-world use. That means taking note of a watch's battery life while using it in our daily lives, evaluating the accuracy of a fitness tracker during a long run, and considering all of the activities and metrics it can track.
 For the models that were tested in the Tech and Engineering Lab, we evaluated the tracker's performance, measured the battery power, checked the durability, and cross-checked the heart rate monitor. By the time our experts arrive at a final score for each watch, they've collected more than 300 separate data points.

 ✔️ Ease of use: This evaluation begins right out of the box by noting how easy the fitness tracker or watch is to set up, including how intuitive it is to operate the device and how seamless it is to use the watch with its app, if applicable. Once the tracker is up and running, our experts assess how simple it is to navigate and check for notifications. They also pay attention to overall comfort, including the strap design.

 ✔️ Durability: This consists of two main tests in the Tech & Engineering Lab. There's the drop test, in which we drop fitness trackers from 30 inches (the height of a typical countertop), then check to see that they're still fully functional. After that comes the water-resistance test: We put each tracker in approximately 8 inches of water for one minute to simulate full submersion; we then wait 24 hours before checking for functionality. A tracker that fails either test is automatically disqualified from our list of recommendations.

 Isabella Cavallo/Good Housekeeping Institute 
 ✔️ Performance: This is the most heavily weighted part of our evaluation. We consider the overall functionality of each fitness tracker and watch, including the total number of performance features. Our engineers also measure battery life and the accuracy of the device's pedometer and heart monitor, when relevant. Finally, we check to see that any smart features function seamlessly, without glitches or syncing issues.
 What to look for when shopping for the best fitness tracker or watch
 When buying a fitness watch, there are a few features and characteristics that you should consider before making a purchase:
 ✔️ Water resistance: If you're planning on swimming while wearing your watch, make sure the watch is water-resistant. Be certain to check that it can be used while swimming, note the maximum depth the watch can handle, and look to see if there are any time restrictions. Some watches are water-resistant, but they can be submerged underwater only to a specific depth, and some may have a time limit for submersion.
 ✔️ Budget: Fitness trackers and watches generally range in price from $100 to $500 or more. Typically, you'll get more features with pricier models, so make sure you'll actually use the features if you're going to spend more.
 ✔️ Design: Some watches look more stylish, and others look more rugged. Consider how often you'll be wearing the watch—if you'll only be wearing it to work out, a bulkier design may be suitable, but if you plan to wear it every day to work, dinner, and nights out, you may want something a little more elevated. The size of the band and watch face can also impact how easy it is to read metrics and how stylish or subtle the watch is.

 ✔️ Comfort and fit: Fitness trackers and watches come in different shapes and sizes. If you have small wrists, you may want to look for a slimmer or smaller watch face, so it doesn't feel clunky. You'll also want to consider your tracker's band to make sure it's workout-friendly and easy to clean. Silicone versus fabric bands can also feel more comfortable depending on the activity (I prefer silicone for swimming, but I find a fabric band more comfortable for day-to-day wear).
 Isabella Cavallo / Good Housekeeping Institute 
 ✔️ Battery life: It's important to consider battery life if you don't like the hassle of charging your fitness tracker frequently or if you often forget to charge your tracker or watch. Claimed battery life has a wide range and can be anywhere around 18 hours (requiring daily charging) or up to a month. If you plan to track your sleep with the watch, a longer battery life and quicker charge time will be more ideal for you.

 ✔️ GPS: Built-in GPS comes in handy for fitness applications, such as tracking your hiking or running route and measuring distance and pace. However, watches with GPS often come with a higher price tag, so be sure you want these features if you're going to splurge on GPS. For trackers without built-in GPS, you may be able to connect to your smartphone's GPS to track these metrics, but you'll need your phone by your side for this to work properly. Some watches (like the Garmin Forerunner 265S ) can even map out a running or biking course for you and give live directions so that you don't get lost on a long run. My Garmin Venu 3S automatically uploads my hiking and running routes to Strava , which is one of our favorite workout apps .
 ✔️ App features: While many fitness watches have a screen that allows you to start a workout, check your steps, and monitor your heart rate, each tracker's app typically provides more analytics. Some may provide free workout classes, while others can enable you to create training programs to follow on your next run. For certain watches, the compatible apps are necessary to get the full extent of the watches.

 The best fitness trackers do far more than count steps. Today's wearables can help you understand how well you've slept, whether you're recovered enough to train, how your heart is performing and even when it's time to take a rest day. Better still, you don't need to spend flagship smartwatch money to benefit from those insights.
 The category has evolved dramatically over the last few years, too. Alongside familiar fitness bands, you'll now find lightweight GPS watches, discreet smart rings and even screen-free trackers that quietly collect health data without constantly demanding your attention. Choosing the right one is less about finding the device with the longest feature list and more about finding the one that fits your lifestyle.
 Our team has spent more than a decade testing fitness trackers, smartwatches and wearable technology from Garmin , Apple , Fitbit , Samsung , Amazfit and many more. We judge every device on tracking accuracy, battery life, comfort, software, training tools and overall value, wearing each one for weeks before deciding whether it deserves a place in this guide.
